item.title: Dungeon crawler demo
item.description: A short grid-based first-person dungeon crawler, in the style of the classic Dungeon Master / Eye of the Beholder games — built with a coding agent as a "can we actually do this in plain HTML/CSS/JS" experiment, not a career section. Movement is tile-by-tile, turning is in 90° steps, and the view is redrawn from a small lookup table of wall segments rather than any real 3D — the same trick those original games used.

item.title: NMR spectrometer temperature drift
item.description: My final-year MChem project at the University of Manchester, supervised by Prof. Gareth Morris and working with Paul Bowyer, programmed a Varian NMR spectrometer to investigate a subtle source of error: the building's air-conditioning cycled on and off every few minutes, nudging the probe temperature up and down, which in turn shifted the phase and frequency of the NMR signal. Because the aircon cycle is periodic rather than random, that drift doesn't average out like ordinary noise — in a 2D spectrum it shows up as a coherent artefact, a faint diagonal running parallel to a real peak. The fix was simple once identified: randomise the order in which the experiment's increments are acquired, so the drift no longer lines up with anything. The diagram below runs the same 24-increment experiment twice — once acquired in order, once shuffled — against the same underlying temperature drift.

item.title: Ozone layer & the Montreal Protocol
item.description: My third-year undergraduate project (on a straight chemistry BSc this would have been the final-year project) covered the chemistry of the ozone layer and the effect of the Montreal Protocol on the Antarctic ozone hole. It followed on from a bonus GCSE in geology I picked up along the way, and a few geology units taken during the degree — a small return to earth science after giving up geography at school in favour of maths, physics and chemistry A-levels. I remember this project less well than the NMR one, but the chemistry has stuck.

item.title: Test cricket
item.description: Test cricket gets written off as boring by people who've only ever seen the highlights — five days, no fixed number of overs, long stretches where nothing looks like it's happening. But the scoreboard is the least interesting part of it. Underneath a session that looks stationary — same total, same batters, nobody out — the balance of the game is usually moving: a bowler settling into a spell, a batter starting to middle it, a declaration being quietly set up three sessions in advance.

item.title: Tour de France
item.description: The Tour de France gets the same complaint as Test cricket: three weeks, and most days end with the same peloton crossing the line together looking like nothing happened. But a Grand Tour is really three or four different competitions running at once inside the same race — sprinters fighting for stage wins that barely touch the overall standings, a handful of general-classification riders quietly managing gaps of a few seconds through weeks of stages that don't matter to them at all, until a mountain stage or a time trial reshuffles everything in one afternoon.

item.title: Weather text generation
item.description: A job advertised as 50% science, 50% programming — in practice it was close to 100% programming, and it's what completed my move from scientist to programmer. The main work was turning structured weather data into natural-language forecast text under hard constraints, for example a forecast that had to fit inside a single SMS message. This was pre-LLM, rule-based text generation: fixed templates and branching rules, not a statistical model. The diagram below runs one forecast through that pipeline — watch the draft text blow through its 160-character budget and get trimmed back down to fit.

item.title: Witron
item.description:
I spent time working at Witron, a distribution centre logistics company. Stock arrives by lorry, gets put away into storage, is picked against an order, then loaded onto an outbound lorry and leaves for a store. The animation below loops that journey continuously, with a live log alongside it narrating each step as it happens.

  2. 08:05 — Pallet unloaded, staged for putaway
  3. 08:11 — Stored — bay B-14
  4. 08:12 — Inbound lorry departs
  5. 09:47 — Pick generated — order #4521
  6. 09:49 — Picked from bay B-14
  7. 09:52 — Staged for outbound loading
  8. 10:15 — Outbound lorry arrives — Dock 7

  10. 10:22 — Departs for store
